text: Use your brain for a second. If a game is fair, you will have an equal chance to win or lose since neither side will have an advantage. That means you have a 50% chance to win. That is literally all it means, and is how literally all matchmaking works. You're basically asking that games should never, ever be fair and one side should by default always have an advantage. Even when everyone is of equal skill, you're asking for one side to get an arbitrary buff at the start of the game to make them stronger. You do realize how stupid that is, right? 50% win rate isn't a forced goal, it's the natural conclusion of all properly working matchmaking. If you're better than the opponent, you will have a higher chance to win and the game is not fair. This causes you to climb to a point where you're against people equal to your skill so you will get fair games (meaning a 50% win rate). If you're worse than the opponent, it's the same but demoting you downwards instead.

text: League boomer here, I've been first timing new champs in Ranked since Xin Zhao release, and he was the first champ released once Ranked became available Over the years, new champions feel really good. In modern League, walking, auto attacking, skillshots, and pathing all feel pretty good. There's the occasional hiccup with minion block, but not nearly as bad as when they were figuring it out Now on to the new stuff. I spend <5 mins in practice tool and I'm ready to take new champs into ranked. I try out a few combos, a few items, and level up abilities to feel the CD. I don't think that's even necessary since practice tool is new. Because of how much the playerbase has improved, the actual champion you pilot takes a bit less importance. You still have your role's job, same roam timers, obj timers, gameplay loop, etc. For build, it's not hard to look down and see if the numbers are Blue or Orange. You've certainly played that class of champion before. And abilities all have an expected range, missile speed, etc. And if something surprises you, you pretty much learn it on the spot Advantages: Your opponent is more unfamiliar with new champ playstyle, CDs, combos, etc. As the player, you become familiar with it much faster than they are. Both of you are unfamiliar with it, but the delta in rate of familiarity heavily favors the player on the new champ You don't choose a new champ and go 0/13. You went 0/13 because of positioning and macro decisions. And honestly, you see plenty of 0/13s anyways on players with 1 million mastery At the very least, your ally playing the new champ for the first time isn't on autopilot. They are actually Locke'd in and reading their ability tooltips, thinking about items, and thinking about their positioning in teamfights Literally on Game 2 with new champ, you have SO much more experience than everyone else playing. The only other ppl with the same amount of exp seeing the champ in their games are the other first timers Why is the enemy Locke always 12/1 coming out of lane? Because he's on his 3rd game, and your midlaner is fighting him for the 1st time. Everyone in this game knows how to adjust around a fed Master Yi. In the first week, almost no one knows how to fight the fed Locke. Once you learn how to win the first ~8 mins, you can just start steam rolling the game TLDR: At least the new champ player isn't on autopilot & the enemy team has no experience shutting down a fed new champ

text: Gold efficiency, as I'm sure most of you know, calculates the gold value in stats of an item, and compares that value to the item's cost. But gold efficiency alone is not enough to judge an items power, even if we ignore item actives. Gold efficiency is a useful thing to calculate, but it isn't enough. Some problems with Gold efficiency: Gold efficiency ignores how useful that stat actually is, especially in conjunction with the other stats on the item, a champion's kit, and a bunch of other factors Gold efficiency derives the gold value of a stat based on other items. So every stat is only measured relative to it's cheapest option. Point 2 is particularly relevant. It's totally plausible Riot uses different timing curves for different types of stats. If, for example, health is intended by design to be easy to buy a small amount for cheap, but magic penetration is not (and thus small amounts are more expensive), then that could make magic penetration legendaries and mythics look very gold efficient, whereas it would make health items look inefficient. Personally, I think this particular example is true. It's a large reason (aside from the passives) why Void Staff is ~130% gold efficient, but Warmog's is only 100%. Health is efficiently purchased with ruby crystals, but magic pen is very inefficiently purchased with blighting jewel. Another good way to see the limits of gold efficiency in this way is to consider the following hypothetical - Let's say Riot decides that assassins spike too hard too early with serrated dirk. So they make the item less efficient somehow. That change will impact that gold efficiency cost of every item with lethality, making those items more gold efficient. Even though those items wouldn't have changed at all, they'd be exactly as good as they were, they appear better because their gold efficiency has increased. Anyway...Gold efficiency isn't everything.

text: Gold efficiency is all about understanding which items are worth investing in over another item. It's a tool specifically used to compare multiple items to each other. The problem comes when someone uses gold efficiency not to compare two items, but just to say an item is too good / bad. Seekers is a good example here. If as a mage I need an armor item, i have one choice, seekers into zhonya's. It could be twice as gold efficient, or half as gold efficient, i'll probably still buy it because there's no other item that gives me those needed stats for that situation. The only other option is to buy a few cloth armors and go for mythic, which would be a very sad state of affairs. Now look at serrated dirk, Assassins don't exactly need pen, but they value it. They do need AD, so they look at caufields Warhammer, pickaxe, BF sword, dirk. And what all those items build into. Dirk gets the most damage for their gold so they choose that. They could choose to be defensive by going for a maw item, and it wouldn't be a wrong choice, but it wouldn't be as strong as taking control of the lane. Mages don't have an item with that much damage boost until they finish their mythic, since they can't win with offense they need to choose defensive seekers and delay their power spike.

text: I think almost all games are winnable, even with huge gold deficits. Though the potential of this is greatly influenced by elo and champions. text: League is extremely balanced. Win rates are kept in an incredibly tight range and any deviation from that sees very swift nerfs. The state of League's balance puts almost every other competitive, asymmetric game to shame. The problem is that League is poorly designed as a gameplay experience. Balance and design (i.e. game experience) are two different (but often related) things. Aside from the frustrating gameplay loop, God-awful new player experience, horrible matchmaking and ranked system, and predatory mobile game-like design of recent years, champion design is often oppressive, overly stacked with abilities, and frequently incredibly un-fun to play against. Kassadin, Zed, Azyr, Yasuo, Yone, Yuumi, Ksante, Zeri, Mel, and this list could go on and on. There are so many champions that warp the game in fundamentally oppressive and un-fun ways for their opponents, even if balance-wise they are statistically fine. With League approaching 200 champions, this isn't incredibly surprising, as it gets progressively more difficult to design new champions and not wander into this territory, but it's also something that a lot of people refuse to acknowledge. In many other games, if the only answer is to chain CC someone until they're dead, that is considered bad gameplay design. In many other games, if infinite chain CC is even possible, that is considered un-fun game design. In many other games, if a basic ability hard-counters and completely shuts down entire kits or playstyles, it's considered oppressive game design. League has all of this in spades.
label: analysis

text: I’m tired of living like a caveman. 90% of the frustration in this game comes from players not being on the same page and typing past each other. If the jungler could simply explain their pathing before ganking, it would drastically reduce unnecessary toxicity and misunderstandings. Basic coordination would be so much smoother. Jungling is already demanding with all these extra objective that have been added. Laning is also demanding—top, mid, and ADC are focused on CS, trading, and wave control. Expecting them to also type in the middle of fights or crucial moments is unrealistic. This makes simple communication harder than it needs to be. Every other competitive game has voice chat. Even Dota 2, Riot’s direct competitor, has it. League’s player base doesn’t have some uniquely cursed level of toxicity compared to other games—if anything, the lack of voice chat exacerbates the problem because players are forced to communicate inefficiently through text, which is slower, less nuanced, and easy to misinterpret. At this point, the lack of voice chat is actively preventing new players from joining and staying. League is already one of the hardest games to learn, with no proper tutorial, and without clear communication, new players are left feeling lost. The veteran player base could be an asset in guiding them, but without voice chat, that experience is frustrating instead of welcoming. Don’t get me wrong. Voice chat should be optional, just like text chat, and muting would be a single button press away. If you don’t want to talk, don’t. But stop holding back a feature that could vastly improve team coordination and has the potential to reduce toxicity. Heck run it live for a week and if its too toxic remove it. It’s time to modernize League’s communication system. Give players the option to use voice chat. If other games can make it work, so can League.
label: analysis
